item.title: Bitter Springs
item.description:
Details

Cave and exploration data

  • Exploration potential: Low
  • Goes to water: Yes

References

  • Trimix Divers - https://www.trimixdivers.com/trimix5/?p=4885: Located near the township of Mataranka NT, these springs have the same source and characteristics as the more famous Mataranka Hot Springs with several notable differences. The water seeping out of the limestone at Bitter Springs comes from multpile point sources distributes over an area of perhaps 50m x 10m. Most are from small holes in the detritus filled floor of the spring’s waterway. None are penetrable. The water is crystal clear with a beautful blue tinge to it. It is a constant 34C and this is warmed by the limestone that holds and supplies it, not by any geothermal processes (same for Mataranka Hot Springs and Katherine Hot Springs).

It is called Bitter Springs because the water actually does taste bitter ! There are no fish living in the water, but there are many turtles, both the long and short necked varieties. The turtles thrive under the vegetation mats that cover most of the upstream waterway. They are quite shy, but we found that with rebreathers we could get very close to them and Paul Boler got some excellent video footage.

References

  • Trimix Divers - https://www.trimixdivers.com/trimix5/?p=4887: This flooded, old mining pit is located in the Litchfield National Park and has been rated by the CDAA as a Sinkhole site. The small lake to 30m provides some interesting diving, although is primarily a training site with good bottom features, some undercutting and plenty of tie-offs. It?s visibility is usually better than Rum Jungle, with an average of 4-5m not uncommon. The site can easily be dived on twin tanks involving a complete circumnavigation of the steep walled sides. Beware of the many sunken trees and line tangling branches.

item.title: Katherine Hot Springs
item.description:
About

Need to dive at night because diver activity silts out the swimming area on the surface

Details

Identification

  • Feature type: Cave

Cave and exploration data

  • Cave rating: Advanced
  • Vertical access: No
  • Exploration potential: Medium
  • Tourism potential: High
  • Goes to water: Yes

Diving data

  • Maximum depth: 10 m
  • Temperature: 32–32 °C

References

  • Trimix Divers - https://www.trimixdivers.com/trimix5/?p=4889: This popular tourist site has 34C water flowing out of the small resurgence at a high rate. The water is crystal clear and its source is the same area of limestone as what supplies Bitter Springs and Mataranka Hot Springs further to the South. The water is geologically heated, but is warmed only by the rock in which it collects – layers of limestone which assume the average annual surface temperature. From the small entrance pool, the 3m2 cave passage descends very quickly down to 8m where it levels to horizontal and reduces in size to about 1m high by 2m wide. The effect of this reduction in passage cross sectional area is to dramatically intensify the water flow rate. The floor looks pebbly, but the rubble is cemented into fine silt and any attempt to pull on a rock simply dislodges it. The walls and ceiling are a loose, shaly type of construction and movement in this passage, against the flow is exhausting. After 20m of straight, horizontal passage, the end of the first ever penetration is found, tied off to a rock in the floor. A chromed metal clip connects the second length of guide line onto the first and the passage then slopes up to the left (SE) where a low flat restriction is encountered. Squeezing up through this restriction against very high water flow was very difficult and the second line is tied off in a wider area and small junction above the restriction.

Noting that the water was flowing from the right as well as the left hand passages, the low flow path to the right was followed and this descended through a tunnel in what seems to be denser, darker limestone. Popping through a small ‘window’ where the flow is again felt, the cave does a sharp left hand turn. 20m beyond this point, a low flat tunnel to the left was noticed that probably connects back to the junction. 10m further on and to the right, the water flows out of a low flat restriction which has not yet been penetrated. Some excavation here may be necessary. A very streamlined side mount rig with 7ltr (55cuft) tanks is recommended.

References

  • Trimix Divers - https://www.trimixdivers.com/trimix5/?p=4891: Located some 400km south of Darwin on the Stuart Highway, the hot springs at Mataranka are a popular place for people to stop for a refreshing swim. The swimming area has crystal clear water that remains at a constantly delightful temperature (deg C ?). The pools overflow into a small watercourse that is full of life ? fruitbats, frogs, snakes, ospreys etc.

The water source is within the jungle area at a small hole called The Rainbow Spring. It is not known whether this hole has been penetrated yet. The water flow is quite high and the diameter of the hole such that off mounts will be required for the task.

item.title: Pine Creek
item.description:
References

  • Trimix Divers - https://www.trimixdivers.com/trimix5/?p=4893: OK, it’s out of the bag. NT has a new freshwater dive site located a few weeks ago by Dr Jeff Swann from Darwin. The info he gathered from the Mines Department confirmed a max depth of 135m in the old goldmine open cut shaft of Pine Creek, 224km south of Darwin. It is a large (250m x 700m) site, blue in appearance with good access via the approach road on the South East corner of the lake. Water quality is confirmed as good with plans to make it a public recreation area in the near future. It is certainly considerably healthier than Rum Jungle! On Saturday, Dr Natasha Mitchell, Dr Jeff Swann and I dived the site. Jeff and Tash dived to 56m finding 5m viz in the first 20m opening out to 8m below that, temperature a cool (for NT) 24 degrees. I dived to 72m, finding the step cut mine to continue downwards, confirming the information previously given. Dim daylight was still present at 72m, although lights were required. In our surface interval we used a zodiac, portable sounder and compass to plot the rough layout of the site. Unfortunately the sounder (rated to 200m) would not give us readings past 79m, but we did manage to plot the area it doesn’t read, giving us a good indication of where the depth is. Future efforts will hopefully reveal official plans of the site otherwise a decent survey will be conducted.

On Monday, Jack Martins, Claire Elliott and I returned, Jack and Claire doing an air dive familiarisation to 45m whilst I did a drop to 100m. I conducted this dive on open circuit using trimix 13/44 in backmounted steel 120’s, with air and nitrox in 55 cuft sling bottles. The dive went well although visibility dropped again to 2-3m past 70m, with the step cut almost vearing to vertical for the final 25m, making for a rapid drop and increased narcosis. A bounce profile confirmed that the site continues further downwards. The return to the surface during the 71 minute dive included Pyle deepstops commencing at 60m, air between 60m and 15m stops, and nitrox 60 stops commencing at 12m. Dive planning software utilised was Z-Plan 103, turnaround at the max depth was commenced 7 minutes into the dive, 18 minutes extra deco time was added to the stops for safety.

item.title: Rum Jungle Lake
item.description:
Details

Identification

  • Feature type: Sinkhole

Cave and exploration data

  • Cave rating: Basic
  • Vertical access: No
  • Exploration potential: Low
  • Goes to water: Yes

Diving data

  • Maximum depth: 60 m
  • Water type: Fresh
  • Tidal: No

References

  • Trimix Divers - https://www.trimixdivers.com/trimix5/?p=4895: This flooded, old mining pit is located in the Litchfield National Park and has been rated by the CDAA as a Sinkhole site. The notoriety of this site stems from its alleged previous life as an open cut uranium mine. The truth is that whilst trace elements were found in the ore extracted, it was not in sufficient concentrations to warrant its mining, however Copper Sulphate abounded and this is the real origin of the site. Whilst the former?s radioactivity remains at very safe levels, the latter remains of some concern from it?s formation of a layer of hydrogen sulphide, which has been known to affect some divers. The site is deemed to be safe by the local council and indeed is a popular swimming hole for locals (2 legged not 4, and not the big chomping types !).

This site makes a superb training venue for depth and low visibility, and drops to 56m near the middle of the lake, beneath the permanent buoy. The sides of the site drop evenly and there is little evidence of any undercuts or horizontal drives from the mining activity. There is a distinct halo- and thermo-cline at around 7-9m above which the water is warmish (27 degrees) and green with low viz, below which the light cannot penetrate and viz opens to 2m, 3m on a good day. The floor is thick fluffy silt with virtually no features bar the occasional 44 gallon drum.

item.description:

Identification

  • Feature type: Cave

Cave and exploration data

  • Vertical access: No
  • Exploration potential: Medium
  • Tourism potential: High

References

  • Trimix Divers - https://www.trimixdivers.com/trimix5/?p=4897: Tolmer Falls is located within Litchfield Park west of the township of Bachelor (90km south of Darwin). The Falls have formed in what appears to be a sinkhole of substantial proportions, some 40m in diameter with 50m high vertical walls. (see photos) Water falls into the sink via a series of carved canyons from the tableland above. There is a cave under the falls (see photo) with a thermal spring and a large bat colony that live in small cave tunnels high on the wall.
